mcqs.question: A platform flags 20M items/day for human review, but reviewers can realistically handle only a few million decisions/day combined. What does this imply about queue design?
options: Since the queue will structurally exceed human capacity, prioritization of which items get reviewed first becomes the central design question, not just a nice-to-have
Hire enough reviewers to clear the full 20M/day backlog, since prioritization is a secondary concern
Reduce automated flagging until the flagged volume matches reviewer capacity exactly
Route the entire 20M/day queue through a second automated pass instead of any human review
mcqs.explanation: Hiring enough reviewers to clear 20M/day is explicitly ruled out by the numbers as impractical, and lowering flagging thresholds would let real violations through untouched. Since the queue permanently exceeds capacity, prioritization — not raw hiring or threshold tuning — is the real lever; skipping human review by adding another automated pass forfeits judgment on genuinely ambiguous content.

mcqs.question: Why is first-come-first-served a poor default for prioritizing the human review queue?
options: It's actually the best default, since it treats every piece of content fairly regardless of reach

A rapidly-spreading, plausibly-violating post causes far more harm the longer it stays unreviewed than a low-visibility one, so review order should weight virality and violation confidence, not arrival time
First-come-first-served is technically impossible to implement in a priority queue
Review order doesn't matter at all since every item is eventually reviewed
mcqs.explanation: Because the queue can't be fully drained, the order items are reviewed in determines real-world harm — a spreading violation left unreviewed causes ongoing damage that a static, low-reach post doesn't. FIFO ignores this entirely. Priority queues can implement any ordering, including FIFO, and "eventually reviewed" isn't true at this volume for every item.

mcqs.question: What's the main cost of running a synchronous, block-before-publish moderation check on every single post, across all content categories?
options: There is no cost — synchronous checks are always free from a latency perspective
It only affects image content, never text posts
It adds cumulative latency to every publish call platform-wide, for the vast majority of content that turns out to be fine, to guard against violations concentrated in a small slice
It eliminates the need for a human review queue entirely
mcqs.explanation: Gating every publish behind a synchronous check pays a latency cost on all traffic to prevent a comparatively rare outcome (a real violation), which is why publish-then-remove is the better default for most content. The cost applies to any content type routed through it, and a synchronous automated check doesn't remove the need for human review of ambiguous cases.
